definition: Noisome means highly offensive, especially in smell.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word noisome. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know noisome should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By late afternoon the fish stalls' runoff gathered along the gutter, and shoppers crossed the lane to keep clear of the noisome trickle.
Unpleasant is the mild rung — a smell you would rather be without, easy enough to wave away — while noisome, at the scale's far end, is foul enough to clear the lane.
Offensive goes further than unpleasant — people complain and keep their distance — but noisome claims the most: foul enough, or harmful enough, to drive them out entirely.

Vile is repellently bad in any way at all — a vile insult, vile weather, a vile mood — and it never has to involve the nose. Noisome is narrower and more bodily: offensive enough, usually in smell, to repel or even harm the people near it.

Sickening names the effect on you: it turns your stomach, whether the trigger is a smell, a sight, or a piece of news. Noisome names the thing itself — so offensive, especially to the nose, that it drives people away or does them real harm.

The castle's noisome moat was its plainest defense and its foulest: two hundred years of the town's drains emptied into water that never moved.
Chroniclers wrote that besieging soldiers who waded it came out retching, and that summer garrisons bribed one another to escape wall duty on the leeward side.
No catapult was ever aimed at the moat, and none was needed.
Noisome is the exact word for that moat, because it means highly offensive, especially in smell — and the especially is doing real work.
Noisome comes from annoy, not noise: a noisome thing harms or disgusts, and most noisome things happen to stink.
It is the broadest of this unit's four foul words, wide enough to cover harmful fumes with no smell at all.

And despite its spelling, noisome says nothing about sound.

In the hot June of 1858, the Thames turned London's front hall into something no one could ignore.
Decades of sewage had gone straight into the river, and the falling tide uncovered banks of waste that steamed in the heat.
Newspapers called the air noisome, and they meant the old, strong sense: not merely bad, but foul enough to drive people off and feared as a cause of disease.
Parliament, whose new building sat right on the water, soaked its curtains in chloride of lime and finally fled a committee room mid-session.
Within eighteen days, lawmakers who had stalled for years voted the money for a modern sewer system, and the engineer Joseph Bazalgette began the work that ended the stench.
